citation: Shyam Agarwal, Courtney Miller, Christian Kästner, Bogdan Vasilescu (Carnegie Mellon University). '3100 Opinions on Code Review in an AI World: Building Causal Theory from Practitioner Discourse'. arXiv:2607.07980v1 [cs.SE], submitted 8 July 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.07980 (PDF https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.07980). Title on the paper is '3100', not '3,100'.
source_tier: Preprint (arXiv v1, not peer reviewed as far as can be told). The authors call the theory 'a proposed explanatory theory, not a validated one'.

date_and_recency: Submitted 8 July 2026. PR-mining: Agents in the Wild corpus links agent PRs opened 15 May to 12 Nov 2025; full PR histories re-scraped Jan 2020 to Feb 2026; agent PRs essentially absent before early 2025, so contrasts are driven by roughly May 2025 onward. Discourse corpus spans 2020 to 2026; coding restricted to 2025 to 2026.
key_claims: Two separate parts. (1) A 'tertiary' motivating PR-mining study on GitHub. (2) The 'primary' contribution: a theory built from practitioner grey literature. Do not blend them.

PR-mining part: agent-associated PRs are merged much faster, attract less review commentary, and are more often seen only by the person who invoked the agent. But no-review share fell from over 50% (mid-2025) to about 12 to 14% (Feb 2026), near the human rate; the gap in merge time narrowed.

Robustness: the authors say findings depend on defensible analysis choices. The specific flip they document is about independent review (agent as author vs agent as tool; mean of per-project proportions vs per-project-month distribution among reviewed PRs). Merge speed and thinner discussion are reported as consistent in every month in the authors' own data; the flip is NOT shown for merge speed in this paper. The abstract's wording applies the flip to 'these trends' generally, so the search summary overstates it if read as 'merge speed flips'.

Discourse part: 38,709 documents collected, 3,100 coded, yielding a causal model of 26 constructs and 67 relationships (64 directed, 3 contested). Central claim: review is the control point; AI does not fix the sign of its effect, the team does via reviewer expertise and review process.

Reviewer load propositions (P1 to P3): higher review load lowers review depth (skimming, rubber-stamping) and review motivation (fatigue, burnout); more time spent reviewing than coding is a coping move that also erodes coding skill.

P4: polished, idiomatic AI code ('surface plausibility') lowers reviewer guard and review depth. P5/P6: skepticism raises depth and effectiveness but lowers efficiency. P7: code opacity (lost intent) makes review slower, less effective and less motivating.
P11/P15: comprehension debt, eroded collective ownership and knowledge transfer, reviewer deskilling; negative feedback loops where shallow review undermines future review skill.
P17 and policy: risk-tiered gating can lower latency, blanket gating raises it. Automated review effect on quality and security is contested.
Related-work section: studies on the same dataset (AIDev) report opposite signs for change size, acceptance and review effort depending on agents, repos and thresholds.
headline_figures: Corpus: 38,709 documents (7,630 web articles from 1,437 domains; 31,079 Reddit threads from 43 subreddits), 2020 to 2026. Relevance judge kept 13,469 of 23,631 candidates (57%); restricted to 2025 to 2026 leaving about 9,100; stratified random sample 3,100 (1,263 web, 1,837 Reddit). Codebook: 4,838 codes, 109,951 quotes, from 2,669 of the sampled documents. LLM: Gemini 2.5 Flash; judge agreement with stronger model Cohen's kappa 0.75. Cost about US$0.35 per document.

PR sample: 2,860 of 3,000 sampled repos retrieved (from 16,317 eligible, non-fork, 10+ stars, with both agent and human PRs in window). Over 2.5 million PRs retained. Merged PRs for interaction pattern: Human n=179,066, Agentic n=8,662.

No human review, pooled overall rate: agentic over 50% in mid-2025 falling to roughly 12% by Feb 2026; human about 14%, stable (Fig 1). Per-project whole-window mean: agentic 34.5% vs human 30.5% (Fig 5). Repos merging all agentic PRs unreviewed: 34% in May 2025, 13% in Feb 2026 (Fig 3).

Author-only review (only human is PR author): agentic 40.1% vs human 21.5% of PRs (mean per-project). Single other reviewer: 4.6% vs 18.7%. Multiple people: 20.8% vs 29.3%. Paired Wilcoxon on per-project author-only proportions: k=1,553, V=418,564, p<0.001, r=0.42.

Merge time: agentic median lower in every month. Agentic median about 20 minutes in May 2025 rising to 2 to 3 hours by early 2026; human median about 5 to 8 hours. Relative gap from more than tenfold to roughly threefold; absolute gap about 5 hours persists.
Discussion: 50.2% of agentic PRs have no review comments vs 37.9% of human PRs. Share exceeding 20 comments per thousand lines modified: 34.5% of human vs 27.8% of agentic.
No-review rate by agentic PR type: test 69%, refactor 41%, bug fix 25%; human feature 8% to CI 14%. Authors read this as projects triaging by perceived risk.
Theory: 26 constructs, 67 relationships (64 directed, 3 contested), 17+ numbered propositions (P1 to P17).
sample_unit_and_population: Discourse part: practitioner blog/web articles and Reddit threads (authors of unknown role; presumed largely software developers but not verified; some may be LLM-generated; vendor posts included). Unit: document segments, each coded by three LLM coder agents. PR-mining part: public GitHub repositories (10+ stars) containing both agent-associated and human PRs; unit: PR, summarised per repo then aggregated. Agent label is rule-based (branch names, bot logins, commit metadata) so 'agent' means agent-associated, not verified autonomy. No control group of non-adopting repos.
observed_vs_stated: Mixed. PR-mining part is observed behavioural trace data (coverage, comment counts, thread participants) and cannot see review depth or off-platform review. Discourse part is entirely stated belief and argument; the authors say it is 'not verified firsthand practice'. All reviewer-load and fatigue claims come from the stated side.
what_makes_oversight_tiring: Practitioners say agents decouple code production from review capacity ('reviewer throughput grows linearly... AI generation throughput grows multiplicatively'). Reviewing is draining because: sustained volume (review fatigue, G439); no author to ask and intent must be reconstructed (code opacity, P7: 'reviewing 5k lines of AI-generated code after the fact is miserable', G978); polished code removes obvious cues so defects are camouflaged (P4); consuming more time reviewing than writing code reduces coding practice and skill. Mechanisms are practitioner claims, not measured.
consequence_for_quality: Per practitioners: skimming and rubber-stamping lower review effectiveness and code quality; fatigue and burnout lower motivation; comprehension debt hurts maintainability, ownership, knowledge transfer and long-term reviewer skill via feedback loops. In the PR data the authors cannot measure defects or depth; they only note coverage, speed and discussion. They explicitly do not test these outcomes.
what_reduces_the_load: Practitioner-reported levers in the theory: risk-tiered review governance (human sign-off only on material or sensitive changes), automated first-pass review (but effect on quality/security is contested and it can lower depth, ownership and knowledge transfer), AI-assisted review that raises reviewer skill, accountability rules ('the AI did it' not accepted as an excuse), skepticism toward AI output (raises effectiveness, costs efficiency), shifting focus to intent and architecture (but risks comprehension debt). Authors say team choices set the sign of the effect; none of this is tested.
limitations_stated: Authors: sources may be partly LLM-generated and are 'discourse about review, not verified firsthand practice'; LLM coding 'can miscode, miss, or hallucinate'; theory construction is author judgement ('a different team could have drawn the constructs and relationships differently'); grey literature 'over-represents vocal early adopters and carries vendor advocacy and post-incident hindsight'; 'a proposed explanatory theory to be tested, not validated'; saturation point cannot be established; 3,100 documents probably more than needed. PR study: agent labelling imperfect; measures do not capture depth, difficulty or off-platform review; observational, 'descriptive contrasts rather than causal claims'; public GitHub only; no baseline of non-adopting projects.
counter_evidence: Within the paper: no-review rate for agent PRs converges to human baseline by early 2026 (cuts against 'agents are rubber-stamped'); merging without review is a minority behaviour at median repo level; agent no-review varies by PR type (risk triage). Yu et al. [26] report within-reviewer habituation (oversight weakening over time) which the authors say runs opposite to their coverage trend. Related work they cite conflicts on acceptance rate, PR size and review effort. Practitioners also argue human review may be unnecessary or delegable to AI review (introduction, P8). Not independently checked beyond what the paper reports.
verification_status: All figures and quotes above were checked against the opened full PDF (primary source) [verified]. The practitioner quotes are the authors' reproduction of quoted blog or Reddit text (handles G###); the underlying blog or Reddit posts were NOT opened, so quotes should be cited as 'quoted in Agarwal et al.' only [uncertain for original posts]. The search-summary claim that 'direction flips' for merge speed is NOT supported: the paper documents a flip for independent review only.
usable_claim: In a preprint (Agarwal et al., CMU, July 2026), a mining study of public GitHub repos found agent-associated PRs merged several times faster and with less review discussion than human PRs in the same repos, and more often seen only by the person who invoked the agent (40.1% vs 21.5%). The share merged with no human review fell from over 50% in mid-2025 to about 12 to 14% in early 2026. The authors say whether review looks more or less independent depends on whether the invoking developer counts as author or reviewer. Separately, from 3,100 coded practitioner blog and Reddit documents they derive a proposed (untested) theory in which heavy review load, polished-looking AI code and missing author intent reduce review depth and motivation, and practitioners describe review fatigue. Present the fatigue and load claims as what practitioners report, not as measured effects.
do_not_use: Do not say merge speed or reduced discussion 'flips' under other analysis choices; the paper shows the flip for independent review. Do not present practitioner quotes (e.g. G439 fatigue) as evidence that review is more tiring than writing code. Do not cite the theory's propositions as findings; the authors say they confirm none of them. Do not say 'agent-authored' without noting labels are rule-based and mean agent-associated. Do not say agent PRs are reviewed less overall in 2026; coverage converged. Do not use per-document counts as 3,100 opinions of 3,100 developers (documents, LLM-coded, some possibly LLM-written). Do not use 'AI agents cause burnout'.
overlap_with_existing_essays: Not checked against the trust essay, Verification Gap or Checking Isn't Catching [uncertain]; this source is new to the research folder as far as known. Likely overlaps in theme (rubber-stamping, review depth) should be checked by the caller.
